reader_question: Which of the eleven routes can carry a reform, and what does each one take?
grade_line: Documented: the Constitution, statutes and official pages behind each route, read on November 11 and 12, 2026; route names and our count of reforms from the atlas, as of October 15, 2026
title: The eleven routes a reform can take run from a city ordinance to a constitutional amendment, and a federal statute, which needs 60 senators to end debate on most bills, is the route the most reforms list, 38.
measure_line: The eleven routes to change in our systems atlas, as of October 15, 2026, with what the Constitution, statutes and official pages require of each, as read November 11 and 12, 2026, and how many of the atlas’s reform profiles list each route
notes: A route’s count is the number of the atlas’s reform profiles that list it; the atlas rates each reform’s chances on its own.
The state and local rows name the examples read, such as California’s signature counts; other states differ.
alt: A grid of the eleven routes to change in our systems atlas, each with who acts, what it takes, how it can be undone and how many of the atlas’s reform profiles list it. A federal statute takes a majority of each chamber, 60 senators to end debate on most bills and the President’s signature, and 38 reforms list it. A state statute is listed by 29, the local route by 15 and a state ballot measure by 11. Executive action and court doctrine are listed by 7 each, a chamber rule or confirmation by 6, enforcement and litigation by 5, civil society by 4, an amendment under Article V by 3 and an interstate compact by 1.
